why: Every other tier measures one point. A point says snapshot --include repository took 102ms;
it cannot say whether that is 102ms on any repository or 102ms on a five-hundred-file one.
The reference fixture holds one Story and four branches, so a read path costing
branches x Stories reads as constant there and as minutes on a real portfolio -- and the
read model does spawn two Git processes per pair.
Twenty times the files, forty times the Stories, three times the branches. Sized by what it
has to show rather than by how large it can be: the subject-index cost follows branches x
Stories and not the file count, so twenty thousand files cost forty more seconds per run and
reported the same 14.21x. Ten thousand still grows the sliced snapshot's own time, which is
the other thing this tier is watching.
Enforced on the subprocess count rather than the clock: a count means the same on a fast
runner and a loaded one, so it can carry a complexity claim that a time budget cannot.
How many times more subprocesses a command may run on the larger repository.
1.0 is the property worth having: the read answered the same question, so it should not
have needed more processes to answer it. status, nextsteps and snapshot already hold it.
snapshotFull does not, and 15 records what is true rather than what would be nice -- a
budget nothing meets is a budget everyone learns to ignore. Measured: 966 subprocesses
against 68, a 14.21x growth. buildRepositorySubjectIndex
spawns two Git processes per branch x Story pair (git show for the record, git rev-parse
for a ref head that does not vary per file), so the cost is 2 x 12 x 40 = 960 of the 966.
That is the same shape as the 975 subprocesses the connected tier's note describes on a
real repository, reproduced here for the first time. Lower this number when the index
reads one tree per ref instead; never raise it.
Deliberately absent. This tier is enforced on subprocess counts, which mean the same on
every host; a wall-clock budget over a ten-thousand-file fixture on an unpinned runner
would fail for load rather than for regression. Times are reported, not gated.
The tier above has no remote, no ledger and one Story, so the entire cost centre that made
snapshot --json take 12.6s on a real repository was invisible to it: 975 subprocesses, of
which 6 were fetches worth 4.5s. It also runs with SINGULARITY_FLOW_NO_NETWORK=1, which
blocks a fetch rather than performing one -- so even a fixture with a remote would have
measured the fetches as free.
This tier has a real (file://) remote, an enabled ledger with intents published on several
branches, and a second capability repository. Network is left ENABLED, because the property
under test is that a read path does not use it.

topology.remoteBranchesNote: Three work branches carrying intents, plus the ledger's own state branch.

note: A budget cannot express this. Time budgets are met by a fast network and blown by a slow
one, which is why the read path was allowed to fetch for as long as it did -- nothing was
asserting that it must not. This counts network subprocesses via
SINGULARITY_FLOW_SUBPROCESS_PROBE and is machine-independent: zero is zero on any runner.
A read answers questions and must not change the repository. The ledger's read queries
each built a temporary worktree to read a few JSON files, so a snapshot wrote an entry
under .git/worktrees, took the index lock, and created a branch it then deleted. An
interrupted read left that behind; two concurrent reads contended for the lock.
